This file is a merged representation of the entire codebase, combined into a single document by Repomix.

# File Summary

## Purpose
This file contains a packed representation of the entire repository's contents.
It is designed to be easily consumable by AI systems for analysis, code review,
or other automated processes.

## File Format
The content is organized as follows:
1. This summary section
2. Repository information
3. Directory structure
4. Repository files (if enabled)
5. Multiple file entries, each consisting of:
  a. A header with the file path (## File: path/to/file)
  b. The full contents of the file in a code block

## Usage Guidelines
- This file should be treated as read-only. Any changes should be made to the
  original repository files, not this packed version.
- When processing this file, use the file path to distinguish
  between different files in the repository.
- Be aware that this file may contain sensitive information. Handle it with
  the same level of security as you would the original repository.

## Notes
- Some files may have been excluded based on .gitignore rules and Repomix's configuration
- Binary files are not included in this packed representation. Please refer to the Repository Structure section for a complete list of file paths, including binary files
- Files matching patterns in .gitignore are excluded
- Files matching default ignore patterns are excluded
- Files are sorted by Git change count (files with more changes are at the bottom)

## File: docs/frontend/README.md
````markdown
# Frontend Notes

## Current Architecture

The frontend is no longer centered on one large pane component. The current structure is built around a thin pane host, controller-backed orchestration, and explicit surface/view boundaries.

- Pane host/facade: [src/app/components/file-pane.component.ts](src/app/components/file-pane.component.ts)
- Pane controller and factory layer: [src/app/components](src/app/components)
- Dynamic rendered surfaces: [src/app/surfaces](src/app/surfaces)
- Viewer hosting layer: [src/app/viewers](src/app/viewers)

The key rule is that `file-pane.component.ts` owns composition and event adaptation, while reusable orchestration lives in controllers, factories, or surface VMs.

## View Operation Parity

All view components must support the same file-manager operations and route them through shared pane-level handlers.

| Operation | List | Grid | Details | Tree |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Single select | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Multi-select (Ctrl/Cmd toggle) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Range select (Shift) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Select all / Deselect all | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Open item (Enter / double click) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Rename selected (F2 / Shift+F6) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Copy to other pane (F5) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Move to other pane (F6) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| New folder (F7) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Delete selected (F8 / Delete) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Drag & drop copy/move (Ctrl/Cmd = copy) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

### Shortcut Baseline

- `F5`: copy to other pane
- `F6`: move to other pane
- `Shift+F6`: rename selected
- `F7`: create folder
- `F8`: delete selected
- `Ctrl+R`: refresh current pane
- `Ctrl+A`: select all
- `Ctrl+D`: clear selection

### Implementation Rule

If a new operation is added to one view, wire it through `file-view-container` and `file-pane` so list/grid/details/tree stay behaviorally equivalent.

## Boundary Rules

- New pane behavior should prefer controller or factory extraction over adding more inline orchestration to `file-pane.component.ts`.
- Surface-specific state belongs to the corresponding surface VM/runtime, not directly to the pane host.
- Browser-facing actions should stay grouped behind pane command objects instead of adding many single-purpose public pane methods.
- If a view-level feature changes list/grid/details/tree behavior, update the parity matrix above.
````

## File: docs/AVI_PLAYBACK_SETTINGS.md
````markdown
# AVI Playback Settings

This file is the current source of truth for AVI-family preview behavior in the app.

Scope:

- `.avi`
- `.divx`
- `.xvid`

Status note:

- The rules below are exact code-configured behavior from the current tree.
- They are not a claim that every combination was manually verified at runtime in this session.

## Current Baseline

As of the current code, AVI handling was restored to the older fallback path associated with commit `a16b456` (`added scripts`) for transcoded preview serving.

That means:

- AVI is allowed to attempt segmented playback again.
- AVI-family segmented playback now uses keyframe-aligned segment boundaries instead of fixed 2-second windows.
- When the app falls back to streamed MP4 preview, it uses the legacy `startAstiavTranscode` / `startAstiavTranscodeReader` path.
- The `mode` query parameter is still attached to preview URLs, but the restored legacy astiav path does not currently branch on it internally.

## Effective Behavior Matrix

| Source | First Attempt | Fallback Plan | Seekable | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Disk AVI | `segmented` | `remux` or `transcode`, depending on codec probe | Yes | Segmented AVI now uses keyframe-aligned windows; if segmented build fails, the fallback URL includes `mode=<plan-mode>` and a 90-second preview window. |
| Archive AVI | `segmented` | `transcode` | Segmented: yes. Fallback: no | Segmented AVI archive entries also use keyframe-aligned windows. Archive fallback preview rejects `start>0`, so streamed archive fallback is not seekable. |

## Exact Backend Rules

### 1. Segmented playback is allowed for AVI again

AVI-family files are included in segmented playback attempts:

- `shouldAttemptSegmentedDiskPlayback()` includes `.avi`, `.divx`, `.xvid`
- `buildDiskVideoPlaybackPlan()` tries segmented playback first
- `buildArchiveVideoPlaybackPlan()` tries segmented playback first

For AVI-family segmented playback, the cache builder now uses keyframe-aligned segment ranges instead of fixed 2-second ranges:

- `shouldUseKeyframeAlignedSegments()` includes `.avi`, `.divx`, `.xvid`
- segment manifests preserve real per-segment start/duration values derived from keyframes

Practical consequence:

- segmented AVI playback avoids duplicate-scene overlap caused by backward keyframe seek into a fixed-size segment window
- segment lengths are no longer uniform; they follow GOP spacing

### 2. Disk fallback mode depends on codecs

If segmented playback is unavailable for a disk AVI file, the fallback mode is chosen like this:

1. If video codec is remuxable and audio codec is remuxable, plan mode is `remux`
2. Otherwise, if the codec is on the transcode-preferred list or the extension is AVI-family, plan mode is `transcode`
3. Otherwise, plan mode falls back to `remux`

Remuxable codecs:

- Video: `h264`, `hevc`, `h265`, `av1`
- Audio: empty, `aac`

Transcode-preferred video codecs:

- `mpeg2video`
- `vc1`
- `mjpeg`
- `mpeg4`
- `msmpeg4v3`
- `wmv3`
- `vp6`
- `vp6f`

Practical consequence:

- Typical legacy AVI content such as MPEG-4/Xvid/DivX lands on a `transcode` plan
- AVI containing modern H.264 plus AAC can land on a `remux` plan

### 3. Archive fallback is stricter

If segmented playback is unavailable for an archive AVI entry, the fallback plan is effectively `transcode`.

Reason:

- `decidePlaybackMode()` only returns `remux` for `.mov`, `.qt`, `.flv`, `.ts`, `.mts`, `.m2ts`
- AVI-family extensions are not in that remux extension set
- AVI-family extensions are in `shouldTranscodeVideoPreview()`

### 4. Restored fallback serving path

The current transcoded AVI fallback is served by:

- `serveTranscodedPath()` -> `startAstiavTranscode(...)`
- `serveTranscodedArchiveEntry()` -> `startAstiavTranscodeReader(...)`

This is the restored older path.

Important detail:

- `startAstiavTranscode` and `startAstiavTranscodeReader` currently call `remuxLoop(...)`
- The `playbackMode` argument is passed through, but is not used inside those functions today

So the exact current situation is:

- plan selection still distinguishes `remux` vs `transcode`
- the restored fallback implementation currently uses the same legacy astiav pipeline for both labels

## Seek Behavior

### Disk AVI

- Segmented path: seekable
- Fallback streamed MP4 path: seekable through the preview URL and `start` parameter

### Archive AVI

- Segmented path: seekable
- Fallback streamed MP4 path: not seekable
- `serveTranscodedArchiveEntry()` returns `400` if `startSeconds > 0`

## Files That Define This Behavior

- `internal/app/stream_handler.go`
- `internal/app/astiav_transcoder.go`
- `frontend/src/app/surfaces/viewer/viewer-surface.component.ts`

## Manual Verification Checklist

Use this section to record what was actually confirmed in the running app.

| Scenario | Expected Result | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Disk AVI opens through segmented path | Canvas preview starts and scrub works | Not verified in this session |
| Disk AVI falls back cleanly when segmented build fails | MP4 preview starts from legacy astiav path | Not verified in this session |
| Disk AVI seek after fallback | Seeking works with restarted preview URL | Not verified in this session |
| Archive AVI opens through segmented path | Canvas preview starts and scrub works | Not verified in this session |
| Archive AVI fallback preview | Preview plays, but seek is unavailable | Not verified in this session |
| AVI with H.264/AAC on disk | Plan may report `remux` | Not verified in this session |
| Legacy Xvid/DivX AVI on disk | Plan is expected to report `transcode` | Not verified in this session |
````

## File: docs/BACKEND_REORGANIZATION_PLAN.md
````markdown
# Backend Reorganization Plan

## Goal

Reorganize the Go backend into a structure that is easier to maintain, easier to onboard into, and safer to extend, without breaking current Wails bindings or archive/filesystem behavior.

This plan is intentionally incremental. The backend already completed the first major refactor step: large behaviors were split into service-oriented files while `App` remained the Wails binding boundary. The next step is to turn that file split into a clearer package and directory structure.

## Current Assessment

The backend is in a better state than a typical single-file Wails app:

- archive behavior is already split across focused files
- filesystem, navigation, workspace, batch, directory stream, runtime, and utility behavior already have service seams
- `App` mostly acts as a composition root and Wails delegate surface

The main weaknesses are now mostly residual rather than structural:

- the repository root still holds thin bootstrap, alias, and OS-launch edge files
- platform-specific process launch remains root-adjacent because it is tightly coupled to executable/bootstrap concerns
- some compatibility aliases remain in `main` for wire-type stability

## Professional Target Shape

The backend should evolve toward this structure:

```text
internal/
  app/
    app.go
    runtime.go
    bindings_*.go
    events.go
  archive/
    service.go
    browse.go
    read.go
    extract.go
    rewrite.go
    copy.go
    move.go
    types.go
    helpers.go
  filesystem/
    service.go
    listing.go
    readwrite.go
    filters.go
    stat.go
  navigation/
    service.go
    manager.go
  workspace/
    service.go
    manager.go
  batch/
    service.go
    operations.go
    types.go
  elevation/
    session.go
    helper.go
    client.go
    platform_windows.go
    platform_unix.go
  runtime/
    dir_stream.go
    pane_watch.go
    filedrop_windows.go
  utility/
    service.go
    clipboard_windows.go
    clipboard_stub.go
  platform/
    system.go
    special_folders*.go
    pathutils.go
    platform_*.go
    platform_times_*.go
    trash_*.go
  ops/
    operations.go
  contracts/
    types.go

vfs/
  ...

cmd/
  wails-app/
    main.go
```

This is the professional end state because it separates:

- Wails binding concerns
- domain services
- runtime/process integration
- platform-specific code
- shared contracts
- reusable VFS infrastructure

## Exact Package Boundaries From The Current Tree

The current repository already has enough service seams to define a concrete target ownership map.

### `internal/app`

Owns the Wails-facing composition root and binding surface.

Current status:

- the whole-type `App` move is now done: the concrete binding type lives in `internal/app/app.go`
- the Wails-facing receiver methods now live in `internal/app/bindings_*.go`
- `main.go` is now the thin bootstrap that builds and binds an `internal/app.App` instance
- the remaining root responsibility is constructor/bootstrap glue in `app_adapters.go`, thin filesystem/elevation adapters, and OS-specific elevation launch hooks

Current files that belong here first:

- `internal/app/app.go`
- `internal/app/core.go`
- `internal/app/state.go`
- `internal/app/builder.go`
- `internal/app/lifecycle.go`
- `internal/app/state_actions.go`
- `internal/app/state_ops.go`
- `internal/app/runner.go`
- `internal/app/services.go`
- `internal/app/runtime.go`
- `internal/app/vfs.go`
- `internal/app/filter.go`
- `internal/app/bindings_archive.go`
- `internal/app/bindings_batch.go`
- `internal/app/bindings_filesystem.go`
- `internal/app/bindings_navigation.go`
- `internal/app/bindings_workspace.go`
- `internal/app/bindings_operations.go`
- `internal/app/bindings_runtime.go`
- `internal/app/bindings_utility.go`
- `internal/app/bindings_elevation.go`
- `internal/app/bindings_vfs.go`

Likely later additions:

- any further moves here would mostly be cosmetic and should be weighed against churn
- app-level event adapter helpers may still be consolidated further if we decide to remove the last root construction layer

Suggested compile-safe batch plan for the full `App` move:

1. move `NewApp`, startup/shutdown wiring, and composition-only helpers behind a new internal app facade while keeping the concrete `App` type in `main`
2. move root-owned non-method helpers that are still referenced by many `App` methods into internal packages first, so the later package flip touches fewer files
3. migrate the `App` type together with the full set of `func (a *App)` files in one package change, rather than moving binding files one by one
4. keep `main.go` as the final thin bootstrap layer that instantiates the internal app package and binds the resulting app instance to Wails

First pre-migration cleanup batch:

- filesystem raw operation helpers: `listDirectoryRaw`, `readFileRaw`, `writeFileRaw`, `deleteFileRaw`, `createDirectoryRaw`, `moveFileRaw`, and `copyFileRaw` in `filesystem.go` now delegate to `internal/filesystem/raw_service.go`
- filesystem support helpers that those raw ops still depend on: `buildFileInfoWithHidden`, `buildFallbackLinkInfo`, and `copyPath` now delegate to `internal/filesystem`; generic path normalization now lives in `internal/platform/paths.go`, and the old root wrapper files for slash-cleaning and parent-path helpers have now been removed
- elevation/filesystem coordination helpers: the old root `opTargetSingle` and `opTargetPair` helpers have been absorbed into `FilesystemService`; platform trash/elevation launch hooks still remain root-owned
- cross-domain helpers that still couple composition to `main`: `classifyError` has moved into `internal/contracts/errors.go`, and nested archive chain resolution now lives in `internal/archive/resolve.go`
- `NewApp` internal-service bootstrap now routes through `internal/app/services.go`, so `main` is no longer the only place that knows how to assemble archive, navigation, workspace, utility, and runtime-stream services
- batch constructor wiring now also routes through `internal/app/services.go`, so `main` no longer owns the `internal/batch.ServiceConfig` assembly block
- `App` now depends on narrow filesystem and operation-manager ports instead of the root concrete types directly, which reduces the type-level coupling that still blocks the eventual package move
- archive-operation adapter wiring and batch error-envelope construction now also live in `internal/app/services.go`, further reducing `NewApp` to callback binding rather than service-specific adapter code
- elevated list/copy/move/delete callback assembly now routes through `FilesystemService` methods, so `NewApp` no longer rebuilds those elevated filesystem adapters inline
- the remaining runtime/service composition hooks in `NewApp` now mostly use named `App` helper methods rather than anonymous closures, which further shrinks the eventual `App` relocation diff
- the `App` filesystem port no longer exposes low-level elevation-target helpers or raw elevated dispatch methods, only the higher-level operations that the composition layer actually uses
- `App` now stores narrow ports for archive, runtime, batch, dir-stream, utility, navigation, workspace, elevation, and pane-watch behavior as well, so most of the remaining concrete-type coupling has been collapsed to constructor-time assembly instead of struct ownership
- `FilesystemService` now also depends on a narrow elevation client provider rather than the concrete elevation service type, which trims one more root-level concrete dependency from filesystem orchestration
- the whole concrete `App` binding type now lives in `internal/app/app.go`, so the Wails-facing surface no longer lives in `main`
- the service-port definitions that `App` used to duplicate in `main` are now owned by `internal/app/state.go`, so the root wrapper no longer carries its own parallel state-interface layer
- state/runtime/service assembly for `NewApp` now also routes through `internal/app/builder.go`, so root construction is down to core bootstrap, root-only adapter creation, and wrapper instantiation
- VFS host state and mount/list/open/unmount behavior now also live on `internal/app.State`, with VFS binding methods now owned by `internal/app/bindings_vfs.go`
- startup, shutdown, and event emission now also route through `internal/app`, leaving root `main.go` as bootstrap-only code
- pane-watch creation/cleanup, dir-stream cancellation, elevation session shutdown, and archive-cache close now also live on `internal/app.State`, trimming more state-only composition behavior out of the root wrapper
- operation start, conflict-event emission, and nested-archive extraction callbacks now also route through `internal/app.State`, leaving fewer state behaviors behind in root helper files
- the old root `App` composition-helper methods are now gone; the remaining root-only construction glue is down to plain package adapters such as the elevated-client launcher and file-info callback
- `BuildConfig` assembly for `internal/app` now also lives in the root adapter layer
- the `App` package flip is now complete: the old root `app.go`, `app_vfs.go`, and `app_bindings_*.go` files have been removed, and `main.go` now binds the internal app instance directly

Why this batch comes first:

- those helpers are shared by many `func (a *App)` methods indirectly through filesystem, batch, VFS, and elevation flows

### `internal/contracts`

Owns frontend-facing or cross-domain wire contracts once they are cleaned up.

Current files that likely contribute here:

- `internal/contracts/filesystem.go`

### `vfs`

This should remain a top-level package tree, not be absorbed under `internal/*`, because it is already a coherent subsystem with its own adapters and archive providers.

Current files and folders that stay here:

- `vfs/unified.go`
- `vfs/osfs`
- `vfs/mount`
- `vfs/registry`
- `vfs/archive`

## Important Constraint

Do not jump straight from the current flat `package main` layout into a many-package rewrite.

That kind of migration usually creates:

- circular dependencies
- duplicated wire types
- package churn without real ownership clarity
- broken Wails bindings during a long transition

The correct approach is a staged migration with compile-safe boundaries.

## Recommended Phases

### Phase A: Finish The Flat-Layout Cleanup

Objective: make the current root-level layout internally coherent before moving files into packages.

Actions:

- split remaining `app.go` Wails delegates into focused binding files such as:
  - `app_bindings_filesystem.go`
  - `app_bindings_navigation.go`
  - `app_bindings_workspace.go`
  - `app_bindings_operations.go`
  - `app_bindings_runtime.go`
  - `app_bindings_utility.go`
  - `app_bindings_elevation.go`
- keep `app.go` focused on struct definition, construction, and high-level lifecycle
- move any remaining non-binding helper logic out of binding files
- standardize constructor patterns and field naming across services

Current status:

- this milestone is now complete and superseded by the package flip
- the Wails-facing `App` type and domain-specific binding files now live under `internal/app`
- `main.go` is down to thin bootstrap/bind flow, and the remaining root app-related code is constructor/adapter glue in `app_adapters.go`

Why this phase matters:

- it reduces `app.go` as a hotspot without introducing package churn
- it makes later package extraction mostly a file-move exercise

Acceptance criteria:

- the root no longer owns the concrete `App` type
- Wails-facing methods are grouped by domain under `internal/app/bindings_*.go`
- `go build .` passes with no behavior changes

### Phase B: Introduce Internal Domain Packages

Objective: move real backend ownership into `internal/*` packages while keeping `App` as the only Wails binding surface.

Suggested extraction order:

1. `internal/navigation`
2. `internal/workspace`
3. `internal/batch`
4. `internal/elevation`
5. `internal/filesystem`
6. `internal/archive`

Why this order:

- navigation and workspace are relatively self-contained
- batch and elevation already have visible service seams
- filesystem and archive have the heaviest dependency surfaces and should move later

Reality check:

- `internal/navigation` can move first in a partial form, with the pure history manager extracted before the Wails-facing service wrapper
- `internal/workspace` is the first slice likely to force a contracts decision, because `WorkspaceManager` owns `WorkspaceConfig`, `WorkspaceList`, and `UserPreferences` from the main wire-type set
- the safe first workspace slice is the storage layer, which has now been extracted without moving the wire-type-owning manager

Rules:

- `App` imports services; services do not import `App`
- cross-domain dependencies must go through narrow interfaces, not concrete `App` references
- wire/request/response types should be owned deliberately, not copied package-by-package

Acceptance criteria:

- service packages compile independently of Wails
- `main.go` and Wails binding setup still only depend on `App`
- no circular imports

### Phase C: Separate Runtime Integration From Domain Logic

Objective: isolate behavior that exists only because this is a desktop app host.

Move these concerns away from domain packages:

- startup/shutdown runtime hooks
- event emission adapters
- pane directory watch orchestration
- file-drop integration
- elevated helper process launch and transport glue

Suggested target packages:

- `internal/app`
- `internal/runtime`
- `internal/elevation`

Acceptance criteria:

- runtime glue is distinct from file-management domain logic
- domain services can be understood without knowing Wails internals

### Phase D: Consolidate Platform Code

Objective: stop scattering OS-specific behavior across the repository root.

Group these under a clearer platform boundary:

- trash
- special folders
- path and filesystem metadata helpers
- process elevation helpers
- file timestamps
- OS info helpers

Suggested target package:

- `internal/platform`

Rules:

- platform package provides capability functions
- domain services decide when to call them
- avoid putting business rules into platform helpers

### Phase E: Stabilize Contracts

Objective: prevent type drift while package boundaries get stricter.

Actions:

- identify wire types exposed to the frontend and keep them in one owned location
- identify internal domain types and avoid leaking them directly into Wails bindings
- stop using generic helper files as shared dependency dumping grounds

Suggested boundaries:

- frontend-facing contracts: one package or one clearly-owned file cluster
- internal service-only types: local to each domain package unless truly shared

## What To Avoid

Avoid these common failure modes:

- creating `pkg/` packages for app-internal code that is not meant to be reused externally
- moving files into folders without changing ownership or dependency direction
- extracting packages that still need broad access to `App`
- duplicating request/result structs in each package to avoid dependency design
- mixing platform helpers with domain orchestration in the same package
- doing archive and filesystem package extraction in the same slice as large frontend changes

## Completion Status

The reorganization is now effectively complete.

What remains in the repository root is intentional:

1. `main.go` as the desktop/bootstrap entrypoint.
2. `app_adapters.go` as the small composition bridge from bootstrap into `internal/app`.
3. thin filesystem/elevation adapters needed to connect OS launch edges and raw callbacks into internal packages.
4. `types.go` as the primary compatibility alias file that preserves stable exported wire names at the root boundary.

That is materially different from the starting point: real backend ownership no longer lives in the root package.

## Current Root Layout

After the `App` package flip, the root is much thinner and now looks more like this:

```text
app_adapters.go

filesystem*.go
elevation*.go
types.go

main.go
```

This is effectively the final intended root shape: bootstrap, thin adapters, and compatibility aliases.

## Suggested Decision

Yes, the backend can be reorganized professionally.

The right definition of “professional” here is:

- thin Wails binding boundary
- explicit domain packages
- isolated runtime/platform glue
- no `App`-centric dependency gravity
- stable contracts
- staged migration with working builds after every slice

Do not treat this as a one-shot folder shuffle. Treat it as a controlled package-boundary program.

## Outcome

The backend now matches the original structural intent:

- `internal/app` owns the Wails-facing app type and binding surface
- `internal/filesystem`, `internal/archive`, `internal/batch`, `internal/navigation`, `internal/workspace`, `internal/runtime`, `internal/utility`, `internal/platform`, and `internal/elevation` own backend behavior
- `main` no longer owns concrete backend orchestration
- the root package is reduced to bootstrap, thin adapters, and compatibility aliases

Further cleanup from here should be treated as optional polish, not as unfinished core reorganization.
````

## File: docs/CANVAS_VIDEO_PLAYER_IMPLEMENTATION.md
````markdown
# Canvas-Only Video Player Implementation

## Overview

The file manager now uses a pure canvas-based video player in the main preview surface. Playback is driven by WebCodecs, frames are rendered into a canvas, and container demuxing is handled through `mediabunny`.

The player is no longer modeled as a browser-native media element replacement. It has its own transport constraints:

- Seekable sources work best when the backend can serve random-access byte ranges.
- Sequential live transcodes can start quickly, but they do not provide full random seeking semantics.
- Decoder recovery after seek must restart from a valid keyframe, which makes stream topology as important as codec support.

## Changes Made

### 1. **New Canvas Video Player Service**
📄 `frontend/src/app/services/canvas-video-player.service.ts`

- **CanvasVideoPlayer class**: Core video player using Canvas + WebCodecs
  - Supports demuxed playback through `mediabunny`
  - Hardware-accelerated decoding via WebCodecs API
  - Frame buffering and canvas rendering
  - Playback control: `play()`, `pause()`, `seek(timeMs)`
  - Real-time state and time broadcasting
  - Container probing for MP4, MOV, MKV, WebM, TS, and generic formats
  - Audio decode and scheduling when the runtime supports `AudioDecoder`

**Key Features:**
- ✅ Format detection across the current canvas playback pipeline
- ✅ Codec support for whatever WebCodecs accepts in the current runtime
- ✅ Direct playback from `/wails-stream` for range-seekable files
- ✅ Sequential playback from live transcoded streams without requiring `Content-Length`
- ✅ Detailed error messages for unsupported codecs, demux failures, or decoder recovery failures
- ✅ Bounded frame buffering with cleanup during playback and seek

### 2. **Updated Viewer Component**
📄 `frontend/src/app/components/viewer-surface.component.ts`

#### Changes:
- **Removed**: HTML5 `<video>` tag
- **Added**: Canvas video player container with custom controls
- **New Template Section**:
  ```html
  <div *ngIf="kind === 'video'" class="video-player-wrapper">
    <div class="canvas-video-container" #videoContainer></div>
    <!-- Custom playback controls -->
    <div class="video-controls" *ngIf="canvasPlayer">
      <!-- Time scrubber, play/pause, volume, codec info -->
    </div>
  </div>
  ```

#### New Methods:
- `videoPlayPause()`: Toggle playback
- `onVideoSeek(event)`: Handle seek bar changes
- `initializeCanvasVideoPlayer()`: Setup Canvas player after view renders
- `formatTime(seconds)`: Format time display in MM:SS or HH:MM:SS

#### New State Variables:
- `canvasPlayer: CanvasVideoPlayer`: Player instance
- `videoReady: boolean`: Canvas player initialized
- `videoIsPlaying: boolean`: Current playback state
- `videoCurrentTime: number`: Current position in seconds
- `videoDuration: number`: Total duration in seconds
- `videoCodecInfo: string`: Detected video codec
- `videoFrameRate: number`: Video frame rate (fps)
- `videoError: string | null`: Error messages

#### New Styling:
- `.video-player-wrapper`: Full-height flex container
- `.canvas-video-container`: Canvas rendering area (black background, centered)
- `.video-controls`: Control bar with seek slider
- `.seek-slider`: Interactive video progress bar with custom thumb
- `.play-btn`: Play/Pause button
- `.time-display`: Current time / Duration display
- `.metadata-info`: Codec and frame rate info
- `.video-error`: Error message display

### 3. **Dependency Inject Canvas Player Service**
```typescript
constructor(
  private api: ApiService,
  private cdr: ChangeDetectorRef,
  private sanitizer: DomSanitizer,
  private videoPlayerService: CanvasVideoPlayerService,  // ← NEW
) {}
```

### 4. **Video Rendering Flow**

```
User selects video file
  ↓
renderContent() detects video extension
  ↓
mediaSrc = URL to stream file via /wails-stream
  ↓
setTimeout → initializeCanvasVideoPlayer()
  ↓
CanvasVideoPlayer.loadFromUrl(mediaSrc)
  ↓
Probe stream/container → MP4 | MOV | MKV | WebM | TS | generic fallback
  ↓
Check codec support via MediaCapabilities
  ↓
Initialize VideoDecoder for detected codec
  ↓
Canvas ready for playback
  ↓
User clicks Play → renderFrame() loop via RAF
  ↓
Decode frames → Buffer → Draw to canvas
```

## Transport Model

The player currently uses two transport modes depending on what the backend can provide.

### 1. Seekable File Transport

Used when the server can satisfy byte-range requests or expose a stable content length.

- Frontend uses `UrlSource`
- Backend can serve `206 Partial Content`
- Demuxer can perform real random-access reads
- This is the preferred path for local files and other seekable sources

### 2. Sequential Transcode Transport

Used when ffmpeg is producing a live fragmented MP4 stream and the backend does not know the final size.

- Frontend uses `ReadableStreamSource`
- No stable `Content-Length`
- No true random byte seeking
- Works well for linear playback and short forward movement inside cache
- Does not guarantee reliable arbitrary backward/forward scrubbing

This distinction is architectural, not just an implementation detail. A sequential transcode stream cannot reliably behave like a fully seekable file.

## Supported Video Formats

| Container | Video Codecs | Audio Codecs | Support |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|---------|
| MP4 | WebCodecs-supported codecs | Runtime-dependent | ✅ Implemented |
| MOV | WebCodecs-supported MP4-style codecs | Runtime-dependent | ✅ Implemented |
| WebM | WebCodecs-supported codecs | Runtime-dependent | ✅ Implemented through `mediabunny` |
| Matroska (MKV) | WebCodecs-supported codecs | Runtime-dependent | ✅ Implemented through `mediabunny` |
| MPEG-TS | WebCodecs-supported codecs | Runtime-dependent | ✅ Implemented through `mediabunny` |
| Other containers | Runtime-dependent | Runtime-dependent | ⚠ Best-effort generic probing |

## Browser Requirements

- **Chrome/Edge**: v94+ (Full support)
- **Firefox**: v121+ (Full support)
- **Safari**: v17.2+ (Full support)
- **Older Browsers**: Canvas player unavailable (would need fallback)

## Technical Details

### WebCodecs API
- Hardware-accelerated video decoding where supported
- Queries `navigator.mediaCapabilities.decodingInfo()` to check codec support
- Decoder resets after seek must restart from a valid keyframe

### Canvas Rendering
- `canvas.getContext('2d')` for frame drawing
- `requestAnimationFrame()` for smooth playback
- `ImageBitmap` for efficient frame storage

### Container Parsing
Current implementation probes the stream, selects a parser, and demuxes packets for the canvas player. For direct file playback this runs over a random-access source. For live transcodes it runs over a sequential stream source with bounded cache.

### Frame Buffering
- Circular buffer of up to 5 decoded frames
- Each frame: width × height × 4 bytes (RGBA)
- For 1080p: ~24 MB max buffer per operation
- Frames automatically released when buffer full

## Known Limitations

### Currently Out of Scope
- Subtitle rendering
- Video filters and effects
- Adaptive bitrate packaging such as HLS or DASH
- DRM-protected playback

### Performance Notes
- Seeking requires decoding from a valid preceding keyframe
- Back-and-forth scrubbing is reliable only when the transport is truly seekable
- Sequential ffmpeg output is optimized for startup latency, not arbitrary random seeking
- Software decoding fallback is possible when hardware acceleration is unavailable

## Testing Checklist

### ✅ Completed
- [x] Build compiles without errors
- [x] TypeScript types correct
- [x] Service injection works
- [x] Template renders correctly
- [x] Styling applied
- [x] Canvas container properly sized
- [x] Real MP4 sample extraction wired through `mediabunny`
- [x] Real WebCodecs video decode wired to the canvas player

### 📋 Manual Testing Needed
- [ ] Load MP4 file → Play/Pause
- [ ] Load MOV file → Verify codec detection
- [ ] Seek to different timestamps in direct/range mode
- [ ] Seek after a decoder rebuild and verify keyframe recovery
- [ ] Verify behavior difference between direct, remux, and live transcode modes
- [ ] Test with various resolutions (480p, 1080p, 4K)
- [ ] Test error handling (unsupported codec)
- [ ] Test with network timeouts
- [ ] Performance profiling (CPU usage, frame rate)

## Future Enhancements

### Phase 2: Audio Support
- Implement `AudioDecoder` similar to `VideoDecoder`
- Sync audio with canvas video playback
- AudioContext for volume/equalization

### Phase 3: Advanced Features
- Keyframe index building for fast seeking
- Frame extraction for preview thumbnails
- Video filters (brightness, contrast, etc.)
- Subtitle rendering support

### Phase 4: Transport Improvements
- Treat transcoded seek as a stream restart instead of in-stream random access
- Add explicit capability flags so the UI can distinguish full seeking from limited sequential seeking
- Evaluate segmented CMAF/HLS-style delivery if arbitrary seek within transcoded playback becomes a product requirement

### Phase 4: Optimization
- Chunked demuxing (lazy-load large files)
- Worker thread decoding (non-blocking)
- Adaptive frame buffer sizing
- GPU memory management

## Code Examples

### Using Canvas Video Player in Other Components
```typescript
import { CanvasVideoPlayer, CanvasVideoPlayerService } from './services/canvas-video-player.service';

export class MyComponent {
  constructor(private videoService: CanvasVideoPlayerService) {}

  async playVideo(url: string, container: HTMLElement) {
    const player = await this.videoService.createPlayer(container);
    const metadata = await player.loadFromUrl(url);
    
    console.log(`Playing ${metadata.format}: ${metadata.width}×${metadata.height} @ ${metadata.frameRate}fps`);
    console.log(`Codec: ${metadata.videoCodec}`);
    
    await player.play();
  }
}
```

### Subscribing to Player Events
```typescript
// State changes
player.stateChanged$.subscribe(state => {
  console.log(`Playback state: ${state}`); // 'idle' | 'playing' | 'paused' | 'ended'
});

// Frame ready notifications
player.frameReady$.subscribe(timestamp => {
  console.log(`Frame decoded at ${timestamp}ms`);
});

// Error handling
player.error$.subscribe(error => {
  console.error(`Playback error: ${error}`);
});

// Metadata available
player.metadataReady$.subscribe(meta => {
  console.log(`Video: ${meta.width}x${meta.height} - ${meta.videoCodec}`);
});
```

## Integration with Existing Systems

### Backend (/wails-stream endpoint)

The backend now serves two distinct classes of video transport:

- Direct files and seekable sources through normal HTTP content serving with range support
- Live transcoded fragmented MP4 output through a sequential ffmpeg pipe

That means the frontend must not assume that all `/wails-stream` URLs are equally seekable.

```go
// Seekable direct source:
// GET /wails-stream?path=/path/to/file.mp4
// Range: bytes=0-1048575

// Sequential transcode source:
// GET /wails-stream?path=/path/to/file.mxf&transcode=mp4&mode=transcode
// No stable Content-Length, no true byte-range seek semantics
```

### Frontend Router & Navigation
✅ No changes. Canvas player works with existing file selection flow.

### Archive Support
✅ Works via `archiveContext` like before. Uses `archiveRead` streaming URL.

## Rollback Instructions

If Canvas player causes issues, revert to HTML5 video:

1. Restore original template (git checkout viewer-surface.component.ts)
2. Delete canvas-video-player.service.ts
3. Remove service injection from component
4. Rebuild

HTML5 fallback code still exists in docs for reference.

## Migration Notes

### For End Users
- Video playback behavior is similar to before
- More file formats now supported
- Playback controls look slightly different (custom UI)
- Performance may be different depending on browser/hardware

### For Developers
- Canvas player is injectable service - can be used elsewhere
- All video rendering now happens in single service
- No more browser quirks with native video element
- Type-safe via TypeScript enums

---

**Status**: Beta - MP4 canvas playback implemented, broader container support still pending
**Created**: 2026-03-23
**Last Updated**: 2026-03-23
````

````markdown
# Canvas + WebCodecs Video Player Architecture

## Overview
A custom video player using Canvas for rendering, WebCodecs for decoding, and WebDemuxer for container parsing. This enables playback of virtually any video format supported by modern browsers.

## Architecture Layers

### 1. Container Parsing (WebDemuxer)
**Library**: `@vscode/webdemuxer` (or equivalent)
- Demuxes container formats and extracts video/audio tracks
- Supported containers:
  - MP4 (H.264, H.265, VP9, AV1)
  - WebM (VP8, VP9, AV1, Opus, Vorbis)
  - Matroska/MKV (any codec inside)
  - AVI, MOV, FLV, TS, M3U8

### 2. Decoding (WebCodecs API)
**Standard Spec**: MediaCapabilities + VideoDecoder API
- Detects device codec support at runtime
- Hardware acceleration (when available)
- Supported codecs:
  - **H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC** (common in MP4)
  - **VP8, VP9** (WebM, Matroska)
  - **AV1** (modern high-efficiency)
  - **Audio**: AAC, Opus, Vorbis, MP3, FLAC

### 3. Rendering (Canvas 2D)
- `canvas.getContext('2d')` for frame display
- Frame-by-frame control via RequestAnimationFrame
- Optional: HDR via Canvas with ImageData enhancements (future)

### 4. Audio Playback (WebAudio / AudioContext)
- Parallel audio track decoding
- Sync with video rendering via timestamps

## Implementation Strategy

### Phase 1: Core Player (Canvas + WebCodecs)
```typescript
interface VideoPlayer {
  // Initialization
  initialize(containerData: ArrayBuffer): Promise<void>;
  getMetadata(): VideoMetadata;
  
  // Playback control
  play(): Promise<void>;
  pause(): void;
  seek(timeMs: number): Promise<void>;
  
  // Rendering
  render(): void;
  
  // Properties
  currentTime: number;
  duration: number;
  isPlaying: boolean;
}
```

**Key Components:**
1. **Demuxer**: Initialize with file buffer or stream
2. **Decoder Pool**: Reuse VideoDecoder instances for efficiency
3. **Frame Buffer**: Circular queue of decoded frames
4. **Audio Sync**: Track presentation timestamps (PTS)

### Phase 2: Streaming & Performance
- Fetch container in chunks (progressive demuxing)
- Lazy-load codec initialization (only decode requested time ranges)
- Cache decoded frame metadata for fast seeking
- Implement adaptive bitrate if multiple streams exist

### Phase 3: UI Integration
Replace current HTML5 video with:
- Canvas surface for video rendering
- Custom playback controls (pause, play, seek, volume)
- Format detection & codec support warning
- Fallback to HTML5 video if WebCodecs unavailable

## Supported Video Formats (Comprehensive)

| Container | Video Codecs            | Audio Codecs        | Browser Support |
|-----------|------------------------|---------------------|-----------------|
| MP4       | H.264, H.265, VP9, AV1 | AAC, MP3, Opus      | ✅ Excellent    |
| WebM      | VP8, VP9, AV1          | Opus, Vorbis        | ✅ Very Good    |
| MKV       | All above              | All above           | ✅ With demuxer |
| MOV       | H.264, H.265           | AAC                 | ✅ With demuxer |
| AVI       | MPEG-4, Xvid           | MP3, PCM            | ⚠️  Limited     |
| TS        | H.264, H.265           | AAC, MP3            | ⚠️  Limited     |
| FLV       | H.264, VP6             | MP3, AAC            | ⚠️  Limited     |

## Codec Support Matrix

### Guaranteed (All Modern Browsers)
- ✅ H.264 / AVC
- ✅ VP8, VP9
- ✅ Opus, AAC

### Excellent (95%+ Coverage)
- ✅ HEVC / H.265 (Chrome/Edge 108+, Safari 13+)
- ✅ AV1 (Chrome/Edge 74+, Firefox 67+)
- ✅ Vorbis

### Situational
- ⚠️ MPEG-4 (requires safari/webkit)
- ⚠️ Xvid (via software fallback)

## MediaCapabilities Probe

Before playback, query codec support:
```typescript
async function checkCodecSupport(config: VideoDecoderConfig): Promise<boolean> {
  if (!navigator.mediaCapabilities?.decodingInfo) return false;
  
  const info = await navigator.mediaCapabilities.decodingInfo({
    type: 'file',
    video: {
      contentType: config.codec,
      width: config.width,
      height: config.height,
      bitrate: config.bitrate,
      framerate: config.framerate,
    },
  });
  
  return info.supported;
}
```

## Performance Considerations

### Memory
- Decoded frame buffer: ~3-5 frames (width × height × 4 bytes each)
- For 4K @ 60fps: ~50-80 MB (acceptable)
- Older files: proportionally less

### Decoding Speed
- Hardware acceleration: negligible overhead
- Software decoding: depends on codec and CPU
- Rule of thumb: 1 frame decode = 1-3ms (modern CPU)

### Seeking
- Fast: Cache last 10-15 keyframe positions
- Rebuild cache on first seek (one-time ~100ms for most files)

## Browser Requirements

**Minimum:**
- WebCodecs API (Chrome 94+, Edge 94+, Firefox 121+, Safari 17.2+)
- MediaCapabilities API (same as above)

**Fallback:**
- HTML5 video for browsers without WebCodecs
- Show explicit "format not supported" for unsupported codecs

## Error Handling Strategy

```
1. Try demuxing with WebDemuxer
   ├─ Success → detect codec requirements
   ├─ Unsupported containers → show error
   └─ Corrupted → attempt repair or fail gracefully

2. Check codec support via MediaCapabilities
   ├─ Supported → decode
   ├─ Unsupported on this browser → offer fallback or explain
   └─ Encrypted → show HDCP message

3. Decode attempt
   ├─ Success → render
   ├─ Codec mismatch → auto-retry with detected codec
   └─ Decode error → show detailed error message
```

## Integration with Current Viewer

### Changes to `viewer-surface.component.ts`
1. Add canvas element alongside existing video tag
2. Detect file format → decide: Canvas Player vs HTML5 video
3. For Canvas Player:
   - Fetch file chunks via existing streaming API
   - Initialize VideoPlayer with ArrayBuffer
   - Render to canvas on RAF
4. Fallback to HTML5 video for standard formats

### Minimal Code Example
```typescript
// New service
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class CanvasVideoPlayerService {
  async createPlayer(
    sourceUrl: string,
    container: HTMLElement
  ): Promise<VideoPlayer> {
    const response = await fetch(sourceUrl);
    const buffer = await response.arrayBuffer();
    
    const player = new CanvasVideoPlayer(buffer, container);
    await player.initialize();
    return player;
  }
}

// In viewer component
if (shouldUseCanvasPlayer(ext)) {
  const player = await this.videoService.createPlayer(url, canvasEl);
  player.play();
} else {
  // Existing HTML5 video logic
}
```

## Migration Plan

**Phase 1**: Add Canvas player for MKV, MXF, AVI (currently problematic)
**Phase 2**: Expand to all supported formats
**Phase 3**: Make Canvas player default, HTML5 as fallback
**Phase 4**: Add advanced features (filters, HDR, subtitle rendering)

## Limitations & Tradeoffs

| Aspect            | Canvas Player                    | HTML5 Video |
|------------------|----------------------------------|-------------|
| Format Support   | ~95% of modern containers        | Limited     |
| Performance      | Software decode overhead        | Optimized   |
| Seeking          | Cache required                  | Native      |
| Controls         | Must implement custom           | Built-in    |
| Memory           | Higher (frame buffer)           | Lower       |
| Dev Time         | Higher                          | Lower       |
| Browser Compat   | Modern only (94+)               | Older       |

## Recommended Libraries

| Library            | Purpose                | Notes                              |
|--------------------|----------------------|-----------------------------------|
| `@vscode/webdemuxer` | MP4, WebM, MKV parsing | Used by VSCode for preview         |
| `ffmpeg.js` / `ffmpeg.wasm` | Full codec suite (optional) | Heavier but maximum format support |
| Native WebCodecs   | Decoding              | Standard, no library needed        |

## Next Steps

1. ✅ Prototype with a single format (MKV recommended)
2. ✅ Measure performance vs HTML5 video
3. ✅ Test codec detection & fallback flow
4. ✅ Implement error handling & user feedback
5. ✅ Gradual rollout to support all formats
````

````markdown
# Canvas + WebCodecs Prototype

## Minimal Working Example

This shows the core pattern for Canvas-based video playback using WebCodecs.

### 1. Core API (Pure TypeScript)

```typescript
// src/app/services/canvas-video-player.ts

import { BehaviorSubject, Subject } from 'rxjs';

export interface VideoMetadata {
  width: number;
  height: number;
  duration: number;
  format: string;
  videoCodec?: string;
  audioCodec?: string;
}

export interface VideoFrame {
  timestamp: number;
  data: VideoFrame;
}

export class CanvasVideoPlayer {
  private videoDecoder?: VideoDecoder;
  private audioDecoder?: AudioDecoder;
  private canvas: HTMLCanvasElement;
  private ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D;
  
  private frameBuffer: Map<number, CanvasImageSource> = new Map();
  private isPlaying = false;
  private currentTime = 0;
  private duration = 0;
  
  readonly stateChanged$ = new BehaviorSubject<'idle' | 'playing' | 'paused' | 'ended'>('idle');
  readonly frameReady$ = new Subject<number>();
  readonly error$ = new Subject<string>();
  
  constructor(private container: HTMLElement) {
    this.canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
    this.ctx = this.canvas.getContext('2d')!;
    this.container.appendChild(this.canvas);
  }

  // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  // Initialization
  // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  
  async loadFromUrl(url: string): Promise<VideoMetadata> {
    try {
      const response = await fetch(url, { headers: { 'Range': 'bytes=0-10485760' } });
      const buffer = await response.arrayBuffer();
      return await this.loadFromBuffer(buffer);
    } catch (err) {
      const msg = `Failed to load video: ${err}`;
      this.error$.next(msg);
      throw err;
    }
  }

  async loadFromBuffer(buffer: ArrayBuffer): Promise<VideoMetadata> {
    try {
      // Step 1: Demux container (you'd use @vscode/webdemuxer here)
      const metadata = this.demuxContainer(buffer);
      
      // Step 2: Check if codec is supported
      const supported = await this.checkCodecSupport(metadata.videoCodec!);
      if (!supported) {
        throw new Error(`Codec not supported: ${metadata.videoCodec}`);
      }
      
      // Step 3: Initialize decoders
      await this.initializeDecoders(metadata);
      
      this.duration = metadata.duration;
      this.canvas.width = metadata.width;
      this.canvas.height = metadata.height;
      
      return metadata;
    } catch (err: any) {
      const msg = `Demuxing failed: ${err.message}`;
      this.error$.next(msg);
      throw err;
    }
  }

  // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  // Playback Control
  // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  async play(): Promise<void> {
    this.isPlaying = true;
    this.stateChanged$.next('playing');
    this.renderLoop();
  }

  pause(): void {
    this.isPlaying = false;
    this.stateChanged$.next('paused');
  }

  async seek(timeMs: number): Promise<void> {
    this.currentTime = Math.max(0, Math.min(timeMs, this.duration));
    
    // Reset decoders and seek to keyframe
    await this.flushDecoders();
    await this.seekToKeyframe(this.currentTime);
    
    // Decode up to current time
    await this.decodeToTime(this.currentTime);
  }

  // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  // Internal: Rendering
  // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  private renderLoop(): void {
    if (!this.isPlaying) return;
    
    const frame = this.frameBuffer.get(Math.floor(this.currentTime));
    if (frame) {
      this.ctx.drawImage(frame as CanvasImageSource, 0, 0);
    }

    this.currentTime += 33; // ~30fps (1000/30)
    
    if (this.currentTime >= this.duration) {
      this.isPlaying = false;
      this.currentTime = this.duration;
      this.stateChanged$.next('ended');
      return;
    }

    requestAnimationFrame(() => this.renderLoop());
  }

  // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  // Internal: Codec & Decoding
  // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  private async checkCodecSupport(codecString: string): Promise<boolean> {
    if (!navigator.mediaCapabilities?.decodingInfo) {
      console.warn('MediaCapabilities API not available');
      return false;
    }

    try {
      const info = await navigator.mediaCapabilities.decodingInfo({
        type: 'file',
        video: {
          contentType: codecString,
          width: 1920,
          height: 1080,
          bitrate: 5e6,
          framerate: 30,
        },
      });

      return info.supported;
    } catch {
      return false;
    }
  }

  private async initializeDecoders(metadata: VideoMetadata): Promise<void> {
    if (!VideoDecoder.isConfigSupported) {
      throw new Error('VideoDecoder API not available');
    }

    // Video decoder config
    const videoConfig: VideoDecoderConfig = {
      codec: metadata.videoCodec || 'avc1.42001e',
      codedWidth: metadata.width,
      codedHeight: metadata.height,
      description: undefined, // Would be populated from demuxer
    };

    const supported = await VideoDecoder.isConfigSupported(videoConfig);
    if (!supported.supported) {
      throw new Error(`Video codec config not supported: ${metadata.videoCodec}`);
    }

    this.videoDecoder = new VideoDecoder({
      output: (frame: VideoFrame) => {
        // Buffer decoded frames
        const canvas = new OffscreenCanvas(frame.codedWidth, frame.codedHeight);
        const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d')!;
        ctx.drawImage(frame as any, 0, 0);
        
        this.frameBuffer.set(frame.timestamp, canvas);
        this.frameReady$.next(frame.timestamp);
        
        frame.close(); // Release GPU memory
      },
      error: (err: DOMException) => {
        console.error('VideoDecoder error:', err);
        this.error$.next(`Decode error: ${err.message}`);
      },
    });

    await this.videoDecoder.configure(videoConfig);
  }

  private async getOrCreateChunk(offset: number, size: number): Promise<EncodedVideoChunk> {
    // In real implementation: fetch chunk from server using Range header
    // For now: stub that would be populated from loaded buffer
    throw new Error('Not implemented in prototype');
  }

  private async decodeToTime(timeMs: number): Promise<void> {
    // This would iterate through chunks and decode until currentTime
    // Placeholder for actual chunk fetching + decoding loop
    if (!this.videoDecoder) return;
    
    // In reality: fetch frames from disk/memory up to timeMs
    // and decode them into frameBuffer
  }

  private async flushDecoders(): Promise<void> {
    this.frameBuffer.clear();
    if (this.videoDecoder) {
      await this.videoDecoder.flush();
    }
  }

  private async seekToKeyframe(timeMs: number): Promise<void> {
    // Query keyframe index to find nearest keyframe before timeMs
    // This requires building an index during initialization
    console.log(`Seeking to keyframe near ${timeMs}ms`);
  }

  // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  // Internal: Container Parsing (Stub)
  // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  private demuxContainer(buffer: ArrayBuffer): VideoMetadata {
    // TODO: Use @vscode/webdemuxer or tsdemux library
    // For now, stub showing what would be returned:
    
    return {
      width: 1920,
      height: 1080,
      duration: 120000,
      format: 'matroska',
      videoCodec: 'video/avc1.42001e',
      audioCodec: 'audio/opus',
    };
  }
}
```

---

### 2. Angular Component Integration

```typescript
// src/app/components/canvas-video-viewer.component.ts

import { Component, Input, OnInit, OnDestroy, ViewChild, ElementRef } from '@angular/core';
import { CanvasVideoPlayer } from '../services/canvas-video-player';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-canvas-video-viewer',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <div class="video-player-container">
      <div #playerContainer class="player-canvas"></div>
      
      <div class="player-controls">
        <button (click)="togglePlay()" [disabled]="!canPlay">
          {{ isPlaying ? 'Pause' : 'Play' }}
        </button>
        
        <div class="progress-bar">
          <input 
            type="range" 
            min="0" 
            [max]="duration"
            [value]="currentTime"
            (change)="onSeek($event)"
            class="seek-slider">
          <span class="time-display">
            {{ formatTime(currentTime) }} / {{ formatTime(duration) }}
          </span>
        </div>

        <button (click)="toggleFullscreen()">Fullscreen</button>
      </div>

      <div class="error-message" *ngIf="error">
        {{ error }}
      </div>
    </div>
  `,
  styles: [`

    }
  `],
})
export class CanvasVideoViewerComponent implements OnInit, OnDestroy {
  @Input() videoUrl!: string;
  @ViewChild('playerContainer') playerContainer!: ElementRef<HTMLDivElement>;

  private player?: CanvasVideoPlayer;
  
  isPlaying = false;
  currentTime = 0;
  duration = 0;
  canPlay = false;
  error: string | null = null;

  async ngOnInit(): Promise<void> {
    if (!this.playerContainer) return;

    this.player = new CanvasVideoPlayer(this.playerContainer.nativeElement);

    try {
      const metadata = await this.player.loadFromUrl(this.videoUrl);
      this.duration = metadata.duration;
      this.canPlay = true;

      // Subscribe to state changes
      this.player.stateChanged$.subscribe((state) => {
        this.isPlaying = state === 'playing';
      });

      this.player.error$.subscribe((err) => {
        this.error = err;
        this.canPlay = false;
      });
    } catch (err: any) {
      this.error = err.message;
      this.canPlay = false;
    }
  }

  ngOnDestroy(): void {
    this.player?.pause();
  }

  async togglePlay(): Promise<void> {
    if (!this.player) return;
    
    if (this.isPlaying) {
      this.player.pause();
    } else {
      await this.player.play();
    }
  }

  async onSeek(event: Event): Promise<void> {
    const target = event.target as HTMLInputElement;
    const timeMs = parseFloat(target.value);
    
    if (this.player) {
      await this.player.seek(timeMs);
      this.currentTime = timeMs;
    }
  }

  toggleFullscreen(): void {
    if (this.playerContainer?.nativeElement) {
      this.playerContainer.nativeElement.requestFullscreen?.();
    }
  }

  formatTime(ms: number): string {
    const seconds = Math.floor(ms / 1000);
    const mins = Math.floor(seconds / 60);
    const secs = seconds % 60;
    return `${mins}:${secs.toString().padStart(2, '0')}`;
  }
}
```

```typescript
// Add to imports
import { CanvasVideoViewerComponent } from './canvas-video-viewer.component';

// In template, add alongside existing video tag:
<ng-container *ngIf="kind === 'video' && useCanvasPlayer">
  <app-canvas-video-viewer [videoUrl]="mediaSrc!"></app-canvas-video-viewer>
</ng-container>

<ng-container *ngIf="kind === 'video' && !useCanvasPlayer">
  <!-- Existing HTML5 video tag -->
  <video class="preview-video" controls preload="auto" playsinline autoplay
         [src]="mediaSrc"
         (loadedmetadata)="onMediaMetadata('video', $event)"
         (canplay)="onMediaCanPlay('video', $event)"
         (loadeddata)="onVideoLoadedData($event)"
         (error)="onMediaError('video', $event)">
    Your browser does not support video.
  </video>
</ng-container>

// In component class:
async renderContent(...): Promise<void> {
  // After determining videoMime...
  
  const videoMime = this.inferVideoMime(ext);
  if (videoMime) {
    // Decide: Canvas or HTML5?
    this.useCanvasPlayer = await this.shouldUseCanvasPlayer(ext, info);
    
    try {
      this.mediaSrc = await readers.streamBinary(videoMime);
      this.mediaMime = videoMime;
      this.kind = 'video';
      return;
    } catch { /** ... */ }
  }
}

private async shouldUseCanvasPlayer(ext: string, info: FileInfo): Promise<boolean> {
  // Canvas for formats that HTML5 video typically doesn't handle well
  const canvasFormats = new Set(['mkv', 'mxf', 'avi', 'flv', 'ts']);
  
  if (!canvasFormats.has(ext)) {
    return false; // Use HTML5 for mp4, webm, mov
  }

  // If browser doesn't support WebCodecs, fall back to HTML5
  return 'VideoDecoder' in window && 'mediaCapabilities' in navigator;
}

## Key Differences from HTML5 Video

| Aspect            | HTML5 Video | Canvas Player |
|-------------------|------------|--------------|
| Initialization    | Instant    | ~100ms to demux & init decoder |
| Seeking           | Instant *  | Decode to keyframe (~50-200ms) |
| Pause/Resume      | Instant    | Flush/reinit decoders (~10ms) |
| Format Support    | 3-4 formats | 95%+ of modern formats |
| Browser Support   | All        | 94+ (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari) |
| Codec Flexibility | None       | Hardware accelerated when available |

*HTML5 video seeking is instant from browser cache; Canvas player requires decoding to keyframe
````
